segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: There are many different factors that influence human behavior.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: One is related to social influence, or the idea that our behavior can be shaped by group pressure.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: To test this idea, a psychologist named Solomon Asch conducted a famous study in the 1950s, which has become hugely influential in the field.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: In his experiment, Asch invited American university students to take part in a simple visual judgment task.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Each participant was placed in a group of seven to nine people, all but one of whom were working with the researcher.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: The group members were shown a standard line on one card and three comparison lines on another card.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: One comparison line matched the standard, while the other two were clearly different lengths.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Basically, the correct choice was totally obvious.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Each person announced aloud which line matched the standard, and those who were in on the study deliberately gave the wrong answer first.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Across 12 trials, 75% of participants conformed with the incorrect answers that people in the group had given before them at least once.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: So they chose the line that was clearly wrong.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: This indicates the strong influence of group pressure.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: This study was replicated in 1980, roughly 30 years after Asch conducted his experiment.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: The subjects in this experiment were British university students.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Interestingly, conformity was much lower with these participants.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: This suggests that conformity may be influenced by culture and the country people grow up in.
